l: the interview between Mencius and king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: The interview concerns the meaning of an ancient kingdom, the king's lack of intimate ministers, and how he should judge candidates for office. Mencius says that the king must investigate the people's opinions before taking action.

l: ministers, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: Ministers in an ancient kingdom are sprung from families noted in it for generations. King Xuan of Qi is told that he has no intimate ministers, and those he advanced yesterday may be gone today without his knowing it.

l: people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: The people are presented as a source of judgment about whether a man has talents and virtue, will not do, or deserves death. Their judgment must lead the ruler to investigate before he appoints, dismisses, or executes the man.

l: candidate for office, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: A candidate for office may be advanced when the people judge him to have talents and virtue, but the ruler must first examine the case. If the ruler finds that the candidate will not do, he should send him away.

l: men of talents and worth, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: Talents and virtue are qualities considered when deciding whether to appoint a man. The ruler should not accept private or official claims about them without investigation, but should examine the case when all the people make the claim.

l: death, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: Death is considered when all the people say that a man deserves it. The ruler must inquire into the case and put the man to death only when he sees that the man deserves death.

l: the killing of the candidate by the people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 7
s: The saying "The people killed him" describes the outcome when the people all say that a man deserves death, the ruler investigates, and the ruler finds that the man deserves death.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 8
s: King Xuan of Qi asks Mencius whether Tang banished Jie and king Wu smote Zhou. Mencius confirms that this is recorded. The king then asks whether a minister may put his sovereign to death. Mencius explains that one who outrages benevolence is a robber and one who outrages righteousness is a ruffian, and says he has heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou, not of putting a sovereign to death.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 8
s: King Xuan of Qi asks Mencius whether Tang banished Jie and king Wu smote Zhou. He then asks whether a minister may put his sovereign to death.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 8
s: Mencius confirms that Tang banished Jie and king Wu smote Zhou in the records. He defines those who outrage benevolence or righteousness as robbers or ruffians and says he has heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou, not of putting a sovereign to death.

l: putting a sovereign to death, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 8
s: Putting a sovereign to death is raised by king Xuan of Qi as a question about whether a minister may do so. Mencius says he has not heard of putting a sovereign to death in the case of Zhou.

l: cutting off the fellow Zhou, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 8
s: Mencius says he has heard of the cutting off of the fellow Zhou. He distinguishes this from putting a sovereign to death.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: Mencius addresses king Xuan of Qi about how he evaluates useful materials and people. He compares selecting large trees for a mansion with employing a lapidary to cut and polish a valuable gem. Mencius argues that a man who has studied the principles of right government should likewise be allowed to apply them. He questions why the king tells such a man to set aside what he has learned when governing the State.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: Mencius tells king Xuan of Qi that a man trained in the principles of right government should be allowed to put them into practice. He questions the king's inconsistent treatment of learned principles compared with his careful use of large trees and a lapidary.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: King Xuan of Qi is addressed by Mencius about his approach to government. He is described as wanting a man to put aside what he has learned and follow him, despite valuing suitable materials and skilled work in other contexts.

l: man, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: The man spends his youth learning the principles of right government. When he grows vigorous, he wishes to put those principles into practice, but the king tells him to set aside what he has learned and follow him.

l: principles of right government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: The principles of right government are studied by a man during his youth. When he is grown and wishes to apply them, the king tells him to put them aside for the present.

l: government of the State, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: In the government of the State, the king tells a learned man to set aside what he has learned and follow him. Mencius presents this as inconsistent with the king's conduct toward valuable materials and skilled craftsmanship.

l: gem, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 9
s: The gem is unwrought in the stone and is said to be worth 240,000 taels. The king would employ a lapidary to cut and polish it.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: The people of Qi attacked Yan and conquered it. King Xuan asked Mencius whether he should take possession of Yan, fearing calamities from Heaven if he did not. Mencius said that king Xuan should take possession only if the people of Yan would be pleased, and otherwise should not. He warned that if king Xuan made their situation more oppressive, the people of Yan would revolt again.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: Qi attacked Yan and conquered it.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: Yan was attacked and conquered by Qi. Its people’s approval was presented as the condition for whether king Xuan should take possession of it.

l: people of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: The people of Qi attacked Yan and conquered it in an achievement described as beyond mere human strength.

l: the people of Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: The people of Yan brought baskets of rice and vessels of congee to meet king Xuan’s host because they hoped to escape out of fire and water. Mencius said they would revolt again if their situation became more oppressive.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: King Xuan asked whether he should take possession of Yan after Qi conquered it. Mencius advised him to do so only if the people of Yan would be pleased, and warned that otherwise they would revolt.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: Mencius told king Xuan to judge whether to take possession of Yan by whether its people would be pleased. He warned that making the water deeper and the fire fiercer would cause another revolution.

l: the conquest of Yan by Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 10
s: The conquest of Yan by Qi was completed in fifty days. Mencius said that taking possession after the conquest depended on whether the people of Yan welcomed it.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Qi conquered Yan, after which the princes of the various States resolved to deliver Yan from Qi’s power. King Xuan asked Mencius how to prepare for their threatened attack, and Mencius explained that Qi’s treatment of Yan had turned the people and other states against it. Mencius contrasted this conduct with Tang’s benevolent conquest and advised King Xuan to restore the captives, stop removing Yan’s treasures, appoint a ruler chosen with the people’s consultation, and withdraw.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Qi smote and took possession of Yan. Its treatment of Yan caused the princes of the various States to plan an attack, and Mencius warned that its doubled territory had not been accompanied by benevolent government.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Yan was conquered and occupied by Qi after its ruler tyrannized over the people. Its ancestral temple was pulled down, and its precious vessels were being removed to Qi.

l: king Xuan of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: King Xuan asked Mencius how to prepare for the princes’ plans to attack Qi. Mencius urged him to restore the captives, stop removing Yan’s precious vessels, appoint a ruler after consulting Yan’s people, and withdraw.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Mencius told King Xuan that Qi’s conduct in Yan had provoked the threatened attack. He advised a reversal of that policy through restoration, consultation, withdrawal, and benevolent government.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Tang is presented as a ruler who exercised all the functions of government throughout the kingdom with seventy li. When he executed justice beginning with Ge, the people trusted him and welcomed his progress.

l: the princes of the various States, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: The princes of the various States deliberated together after Qi took possession of Yan and resolved to deliver Yan from Qi’s power. Their plans to attack Qi caused King Xuan to seek Mencius’s advice.

l: the people of Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: The people of Yan initially believed that King Xuan’s forces would deliver them from oppression and brought baskets of rice and vessels of congee to meet the army. They then suffered the killing of their fathers and elder brothers, the confinement of their sons and younger brothers, and the destruction of their ancestral temple.

l: the ruler of Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: The ruler of Yan is described as having tyrannized over his people. King Xuan went to punish him, but Mencius said Qi’s subsequent actions were improper.

l: the conquest of Yan by Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: The conquest of Yan by Qi began as a punishment of the tyrannical ruler, but it became an occupation marked by killings, confinements, destruction of the ancestral temple, and removal of precious vessels.

l: the princes' threatened attack on Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: The princes’ threatened attack on Qi arose after Qi took possession of Yan and failed to practice benevolent government. Mencius said the rest of the kingdom was jealously afraid of Qi’s strength and was moved to arms by its conduct.

l: Qi's punitive expedition against Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Qi’s punitive expedition against Yan was undertaken because the ruler of Yan had tyrannized over the people. Although the people expected deliverance, the expedition led to further abuses under Qi’s control.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Mencius said that Qi’s doubled territory was not accompanied by benevolent government. He presented benevolent rule as necessary to prevent the other states from attacking Qi.

l: the restoration of the captives and withdrawal from Yan, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 11
s: Mencius advised King Xuan to restore the captives, both old and young, stop removing Yan’s precious vessels, consult Yan’s people about appointing a ruler, and withdraw from the country. He said this course might still stop the threatened attack.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: The unit concerns a brush between Zou and Lu and a dispute brought by duke Mu to Mencius. Duke Mu says that thirty-three officers were killed and that none of the people died defending them, creating a dilemma about punishment. Mencius explains that the people had previously suffered while the state's granaries, treasuries, and arsenals remained full, and that the officers failed to report their distress. He advises duke Mu to practice benevolent government so that the people will love their superiors and die for their officers.

l: Zou, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Zou is involved in a brush with Lu.

l: Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Lu is involved in a brush with Zou.

l: brush between Zou and Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: The brush between Zou and Lu provides the setting for duke Mu's question to Mencius.

l: duke Mu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Duke Mu tells Mencius that thirty-three of his officers were killed and that none of the people defended them. He asks how to address the people's conduct when punishing all of them seems impossible.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Mencius tells duke Mu that the people's failure to defend their officers resulted from the officers' earlier neglect and cruelty during famine and distress. He advises duke Mu to practice benevolent government.

l: officers, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Thirty-three officers were killed, and none of the people died defending them. Mencius says the officers failed to report the people's suffering while state stores and arsenals remained full.

l: people, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: The people suffered during calamitous and famine years, with the old and weak left in ditches and water-channels and the able-bodied scattered. Mencius says they have repaid the conduct of their officers and should not be blamed, and that benevolent government would lead them to die for their officers.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 12
s: Mencius says that if duke Mu practices benevolent government, the people will love him and all above them and will die for their officers.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius whether Teng should serve Qi or Chu. Mencius says the proposed plan is beyond him and advises Duke Wen to dig deeper moats, build higher walls, and guard them well. He further advises preparing to die in defense and ensuring that the people will not leave Teng during an attack.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius whether Teng should serve Qi or Chu. He is advised to strengthen Teng's defenses and prepare to die in its defense if attacked.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Mencius tells Duke Wen of Teng that the proposed plan is beyond him. He advises digging deeper moats, building higher walls, guarding them well, and keeping the people from leaving.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Teng is described as a small kingdom located between Qi and Chu. It is advised to strengthen its defenses and prepare for attack.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Qi is identified as one of the kingdoms between which Teng lies. Duke Wen of Teng considers whether Teng should serve Qi.

l: Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Chu is identified as one of the kingdoms between which Teng lies. Duke Wen of Teng considers whether Teng should serve Chu.

l: the people of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: The people of Teng are to be kept from leaving Teng if it is attacked. Mencius advises that they should be prepared to remain in its defense.

l: serving Qi or Chu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: Serving Qi or Chu is the choice Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius to address. Mencius says the proposed plan is beyond him and instead recommends strengthening Teng's defenses.

l: attack on Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 13
s: In case of attack, Mencius advises Teng to have deeper moats, higher walls, strong guards, and people prepared to remain and die in its defense.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius how to respond because the people of Qi are going to fortify Xue. Mencius recounts that king Tai left Bin because of repeated incursions by northern barbarians and settled at the foot of mount Qi out of necessity. He tells the duke that if he does good, one of his descendants may attain royal dignity, while Heaven determines the accomplishment of the great result. Mencius says the duke should be strong to do good, because that is his business.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: He asks Mencius what course to take because the people of Qi are going to fortify Xue and the situation alarms him. Mencius tells him to be strong to do good.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: He advises duke Wen of Teng about the threatened fortification of Xue. He recounts king Tai’s departure from Bin and teaches that a ruler should do good while leaving the ultimate result to Heaven.

l: people of Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: They are going to fortify Xue, causing duke Wen of Teng great alarm.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Qi is associated with the people who are going to fortify Xue. Mencius says that Qi is not the duke’s concern compared with doing good.

l: Xue, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Xue is the place that the people of Qi are going to fortify.

l: fortification of Xue, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: It is the threatened action that occasions duke Wen of Teng great alarm.

l: king Tai, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: He formerly dwelt in Bin, but repeated incursions by the barbarians of the north compelled him to leave. He settled at the foot of mount Qi out of necessity rather than because he had selected the situation.

l: royal dignity, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Mencius says that if the duke does good, one of his descendants in a later generation may attain royal dignity.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Heaven determines the accomplishment of the great result.

l: doing good, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 14
s: Mencius presents doing good as the duke’s essential business and urges him to be strong in it.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius how Teng can avoid suffering from the large kingdoms on either side of it. Mencius recounts how king Tai faced repeated incursions by the barbarians of the north despite serving them with goods and animals. King Tai left Bin, crossed mountain Liang, built a town at the foot of mount Qi, and dwelt there. The people of Pin followed him, while Mencius asks duke Wen to choose between leaving and remaining prepared to die for the kingdom.

l: duke Wen of Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: Duke Wen of Teng asks Mencius what course he should take so that Teng may avoid suffering from the large kingdoms on either side of it. Mencius asks him to choose between two courses illustrated by king Tai’s example.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: Mencius responds to duke Wen of Teng by recounting king Tai’s treatment of the barbarians of the north and his departure from Bin. He asks duke Wen to choose between leaving and remaining prepared to die for the kingdom.

l: Teng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: Teng is described as a small State situated between large kingdoms on either side. Despite doing its utmost to serve them, Teng cannot escape suffering from them.

l: barbarians of the north, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: The barbarians of the north repeatedly made incursions upon Bin. They continued to cause suffering despite receiving skins and silks, dogs and horses, and pearls and gems from king Tai.

l: king Tai, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: King Tai dwelt in Bin and tried serving the barbarians of the north with skins and silks, dogs and horses, and pearls and gems, but still suffered from them. He concluded that they wanted his territory, then left Bin and established himself at the foot of mount Qi.

l: Bin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: Bin was the place where king Tai dwelt before the repeated incursions by the barbarians of the north led him to leave. King Tai crossed mountain Liang after departing from Bin.

l: territory, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: King Tai concluded that the barbarians of the north wanted his territory. He said that a ruler should not injure his people with that wherewith he nourishes them.

l: people of Pin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: The people of Pin regarded king Tai as a benevolent man and said they must not lose him. Those who followed him looked like crowds hastening to market.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: The kingdom is described as something to be kept from generation to generation. One individual cannot dispose of it in his own person, and he may be expected to die for it rather than quit it.

l: incursions by the barbarians of the north, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: The incursions by the barbarians of the north were constant attacks upon Bin. They continued even after king Tai offered them skins and silks, dogs and horses, and pearls and gems.

l: king Tai's departure from Bin, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 15
s: King Tai's departure from Bin followed his conclusion that the barbarians of the north wanted his territory. He crossed mountain Liang, built a town at the foot of mount Qi, and dwelt there, with people following him.

l: Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Duke Ping of Lu plans to visit Meng Ke but is stopped by his favourite, Zang Cang, who claims that Meng Ke’s observances during his second mourning exceeded those of the first. Yue Zheng corrects the duke, explaining that the differences reflected the distinction between poverty and wealth, not improper excess. Yue Zheng tells Meng Ke that Zang Cang prevented the visit, and Meng Ke says that Heaven determines whether a ruler will trust and employ him.

l: duke Ping of Lu, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Duke Ping of Lu intends to visit Meng Ke but abandons the plan after Zang Cang warns him about Meng Ke’s second mourning. Yue Zheng later explains that the differences in mourning expenses reflected poverty and wealth.

l: Zang Cang, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Zang Cang, a favourite of duke Ping of Lu, asks where the duke is going and advises him not to visit Meng Ke. His intervention prevents the duke from making the intended visit.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Meng Ke is the scholar whom duke Ping of Lu intends to visit. He learns from Yue Zheng that Zang Cang stopped the visit and concludes that Heaven, not Zang Cang, determines whether he will find a suitable ruler.

l: Yue Zheng, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Yue Zheng questions duke Ping of Lu about not visiting Meng Ke and explains that the differences in Meng Ke’s second mourning were due to poverty and wealth. He later informs Meng Ke that Zang Cang prevented the duke’s visit.

l: second mourning, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Meng Ke’s observances during his second mourning are said by Zang Cang to have exceeded those of the first. Yue Zheng explains that the more expensive coffin, shell, grave-clothes, and shroud reflected greater wealth, while the rites themselves differed according to status.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book I (Liang Hui Wang), Chapter 16
s: Heaven is described by Meng Ke as determining whether he will find a ruler who trusts him and puts his counsels into practice. Meng Ke says Zang Cang cannot control that outcome.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius whether he could equal the achievements of Guan Zhong and Yan if he governed Qi. Mencius says that bringing Qi to royal dignity would be easy because its territory and population are sufficient, the people suffer greatly, and benevolent government would win their support. He explains that king Wen faced greater obstacles than a ruler of Qi would face, while Wu Ding and Zhou benefited from established influence and capable assistance. Mencius concludes that the present time is especially favorable for a true sovereign to arise.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Mencius argues that raising Qi to royal dignity would be as easy as turning the hand. He explains that the conditions of the present time, including the people’s suffering and Qi’s resources, make benevolent government especially effective.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius whether he could reproduce the achievements of Guan Zhong and Yan by obtaining the government of Qi. He is perplexed by Mencius’s claim that royal dignity could be attained easily and asks whether king Wen should instead be the model.

l: Guan Zhong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Guan Zhong is described as having raised his prince to leadership over the other princes. Mencius also presents him as a comparison that Zeng Xi rejected because Guan Zhong’s accomplishments were ultimately limited despite his influence and long direction of government.

l: Yan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Yan is described as having made his prince illustrious. Gong Sun Chou presents Yan’s achievement alongside Guan Zhong’s as a standard for what Mencius might accomplish.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: king Wen is described as possessing great virtue but not seeing his influence spread throughout the kingdom during his lifetime. Mencius explains that king Wen began with only a territory of one hundred square li, making immediate attainment of royal dignity difficult.

l: Wu Ding, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Wu Ding is described as one of several worthy and sage sovereigns who appeared before Zhou. He had the princes coming to his court and possessed the kingdom as if he moved it around in his palm.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Qi is described as possessing territory comparable to the royal domain of the flourishing Xia, Yin, and Zhou periods. Its population extends throughout the State, so no change in territory or population is needed for its ruler to pursue royal dignity.

l: the people of Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: The people of Qi are associated with a saying that wisdom is less important than favorable opportunity and that farming instruments are less important than waiting for the proper seasons. Their saying supports Mencius’s claim that timing is crucial.

l: the people, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: The people are described as suffering intensely under tyrannical government. Mencius says they would welcome benevolent government as readily as hungry people accept food, thirsty people accept drink, or people hanging by the heels accept relief.

l: Yin dynasty, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: The Yin dynasty is described as having held the kingdom for a long time, making change difficult. Its established families, old manners, and inherited influence also helped delay Zhou’s loss of the throne.

l: government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Government is discussed as something that Guan Zhong directed for a long period and as the means through which a ruler could put benevolent government into practice. Mencius argues that effective government in Qi could quickly produce royal authority.

l: royal dignity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Royal dignity is described by Mencius as easy for Qi to attain under present conditions. He contrasts this with the greater difficulty king Wen faced because of his small territory and limited initial resources.

l: benevolent government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: Benevolent government is presented as the action that would enable Qi’s ruler to become sovereign. Mencius says no power could prevent this result and that the people would be delighted by such government.

l: the rise of a true sovereign, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou) / Chapter 1
s: The rise of a true sovereign is said never to have been more distant from the present in time, while the people’s suffering from tyranny has never been more intense. Mencius nevertheless says these conditions make the present an especially favorable time for such a sovereign to arise.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Gong Sun Chou questions Mencius about the unperturbed mind, valour, the will, and the passion-nature. Mencius explains that the will leads the passion-nature, and that the vast, flowing passion-nature is nourished by accumulated righteous deeds without forcing its growth. He says he understands words by discerning the condition of the speaker's mind and argues that these conditions affect government. Mencius compares Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and Confucius, concluding that no one has been like Confucius, though Mencius wishes to learn to be like him.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Gong Sun Chou asks Mencius about the unperturbed mind, valour, the will, the passion-nature, words, and Mencius's standing in relation to sages. He also asks how Confucius differed from Bo Yi and Yi Yin.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that he attained an unperturbed mind at forty and that he understands words and is skilled in nourishing his vast, flowing passion-nature. He explains the relation between the will and passion-nature, discusses righteousness and government, and says he wishes to learn to be like Confucius.

l: unperturbed mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The unperturbed mind is attained by Mencius at forty, while the scholar Gao attained it earlier. Mencius says that attaining it is not difficult and discusses different ways of nourishing valour in relation to it.

l: valour, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Bei Gong You nourishes valour by refusing to flinch from physical blows or insults and by fearing none of the princes. Meng Shi She nourishes valour by rising superior to all fear, and Mencius says this is inferior to the more important form maintained by the philosopher Zeng.

l: will, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The will is the leader and chief of the passion-nature. When the will alone is active it moves the passion-nature, while the passion-nature can also move the will.

l: passion-nature, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The passion-nature pervades and animates the body but is subordinate to the will. Mencius says it should be maintained without doing violence to it, and that it can be injured by trying to force its growth.

l: vast, flowing passion-nature, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The vast, flowing passion-nature is exceedingly great and strong when nourished by rectitude and left unharmed. It fills all between heaven and earth, is the mate and assistant of righteousness and reason, and is produced by accumulating righteous deeds rather than by incidental acts.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Righteousness nourishes the vast, flowing passion-nature when it is accumulated through constant practice. Mencius criticizes Gao for treating righteousness as something external and says that the mind must feel complacency in righteous conduct.

l: words, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says he understands words by recognizing the speaker's condition: one-sided words show a clouded mind, extravagant words a fallen and sunk mind, depraved words departure from principle, and evasive words a mind at its wit's end.

l: mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The mind can be unperturbed, clouded, fallen, sunk, departed from principle, or at its wit's end. Mencius says the mind should not forget its work in nourishing the passion-nature, but should not force its growth.

l: government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius says that evils growing in the mind injure government and that, when displayed in government, they harm the conduct of affairs. He also discusses how sages and rulers would act in times of good government and disorder.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Confucius says that he is not a Sage, explaining that he learns without satiety and teaches without being tired. Mencius says he wishes to learn to be like Confucius and agrees that no one from the birth of mankind has been as complete as Confucius.

l: princes, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The princes are used as examples in discussions of fear, insult, and service. Bo Yi, Yi Yin, and other sages are described as capable of bringing all the princes to attend their court and obtaining the throne without unrighteous acts or killing an innocent person.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius explains the difference between ruling through force and ruling through virtue. He says that force can make a person the leader of the princes, but people submit only because they lack the strength to resist. Virtue and benevolence make people sincerely pleased to submit, allowing a prince to become sovereign without a large kingdom. Tang, king Wen, Confucius, the seventy disciples, and the Book of Poetry are cited as illustrations.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius distinguishes between using force to pretend to benevolence and using virtue to practise benevolence. He explains that virtue leads people to submit sincerely, while force produces submission without heartfelt loyalty.

l: force, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Force can make a person the leader of the princes, but it requires a large kingdom. Those subdued by force do not submit in heart; they submit because they cannot resist.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Benevolence is presented as either a pretence supported by force or a practice grounded in virtue. When practised through virtue, it leads people to submit sincerely.

l: leader of the princes, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: The leader of the princes is one who uses force to make a pretence to benevolence. Such a leader requires a large kingdom.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: A large kingdom is required to become the leader of the princes through force. It is not required for a prince to become the sovereign of the kingdom through virtue.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Virtue enables a person to practise benevolence and become the sovereign of the kingdom. It causes people to be pleased in their hearts and sincerely submit.

l: sovereign of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: The sovereign of the kingdom is one who uses virtue to practise benevolence. A prince need not wait for a large kingdom to become the sovereign of the kingdom.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Tang became sovereign of the kingdom with only seventy li.

l: king Wen, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: king Wen became sovereign of the kingdom with only a hundred li.

l: submission, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Submission caused by force is reluctant and results from insufficient strength to resist. Submission caused by virtue is heartfelt and sincere, as illustrated by the seventy disciples' submission to Confucius.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Confucius received the sincere submission of the seventy disciples, which is presented as an example of submission produced by virtue.

l: seventy disciples, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: The seventy disciples sincerely submitted to Confucius. Their submission illustrates how virtue can win heartfelt allegiance.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: The Book of Poetry is quoted as saying that people from the west, east, south, and north did not refuse submission. The quotation illustrates sincere submission.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius teaches that benevolence brings glory to a prince, while acting without it brings disgrace. He says a prince should esteem virtue, honor virtuous scholars, appoint worthy and able people, and use peaceful periods to clarify government and its legal sanctions. Confucius affirms that the Book of Poetry illustrates sound governing through preparation and protection from insult. The passage concludes that calamity and happiness result from people's own actions, while Heaven-sent calamities may still be escaped and self-caused calamities cannot.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius says that benevolence brings glory to a prince and its opposite brings disgrace. He advises a prince to esteem virtue, honor virtuous scholars, appoint worthy people to dignity, and give able people positions of trust.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Confucius says that the author of the cited ode understood the way of governing.

l: the princes of the present day, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: The princes of the present day hate disgrace but complacently do what is not benevolent. During peaceful periods, they abandon themselves to pleasure and indolent indifference, thereby seeking calamities for themselves.

l: a prince, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: A prince who hates disgrace should esteem virtue, honor virtuous scholars, appoint worthy people to dignified positions, and give able people offices of trust. If he governs his kingdom rightly, no one will dare to insult him.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: A kingdom should be governed according to clearly understood principles and legal sanctions during periods of leisure and freedom from external troubles. If governed rightly, even great kingdoms will be constrained to stand in awe.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Heaven may send down calamities that it is still possible to escape.

l: God, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: The ordinances of God are presented as commands with which people should always strive to remain in harmony in order to obtain much happiness.

l: Book of Poetry, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: The Book of Poetry says that gathering mulberry bark and weaving it into the window and door of a nest before the rain can protect against insult. It also says that people should be studious to remain in harmony with the ordinances of God so they will obtain much happiness.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Benevolence brings glory to a prince, while its opposite brings disgrace.

l: disgrace, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Disgrace results from acting without benevolence. A prince who hates disgrace should pursue virtue, honor virtuous scholars, and govern rightly.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: A prince seeking to avoid disgrace should esteem virtue and honor virtuous scholars.

l: government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: A prince should use periods of leisure and rest from external troubles to clearly digest the principles of his government with its legal sanctions. Confucius says the cited ode demonstrates understanding of the way of governing.

l: calamity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Calamity can result from people's own actions. Calamities sent by Heaven may still be escaped, but calamities people cause themselves cannot be escaped.

l: happiness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Happiness is something people seek for themselves. Remaining in harmony with the ordinances of God is said to bring much happiness.

l: ordinances of God, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: The Book of Poetry teaches that people should always be studious to remain in harmony with the ordinances of God, so they will obtain much happiness.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius explains that a ruler can gain the support of scholars, traders, travellers, husbandmen, and all the people by practising five specific policies. These policies include honouring talented and virtuous men, limiting market and frontier charges, requiring mutual aid on public fields without extra taxes, and avoiding certain levies on shop occupiers. If a ruler truly practises these five things, neighbouring kingdoms will regard him as a parent, and he will have no enemy in the kingdom. Such a ruler is called the minister of Heaven and will attain the royal dignity.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius says that a ruler should honour men of talents and virtue, employ the able, and adopt five policies that win the support of the people.

l: ruler, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: A ruler should fill offices with distinguished individuals, limit or avoid specified taxes and charges, and require husbandmen to give mutual aid on the public field. If he practises these five things, neighbouring kingdoms will look up to him as a parent, he will have no enemy in the kingdom, and he will attain the royal dignity.

l: scholars of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The scholars of the kingdom will be pleased and wish to stand in the ruler's court if he honours men of talents and virtue and employs the able.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The kingdom is the realm whose scholars, traders, travellers, husbandmen, and people may be won by the ruler's policies. A ruler with no enemy in the kingdom is called the minister of Heaven.

l: market-place of his capital, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The market-place of the ruler's capital should be subject either to a ground-rent on shops without taxation of goods or to proper regulations without ground-rent. Traders will then wish to store their goods there.

l: traders of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The traders of the kingdom will be pleased and wish to store their goods in the ruler's market-place if goods are not taxed under the stated market arrangements.

l: travellers of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The travellers of the kingdom will be pleased and wish to make their tours on the ruler's roads if frontier-passes inspect persons without charging taxes on goods or other articles.

l: husbandmen of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The husbandmen of the kingdom will be pleased and wish to plough in the ruler's fields if they give mutual aid to cultivate the public field and pay no other taxes.

l: people of the kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The people of the kingdom will be pleased and wish to come and be the ruler's people if he does not exact the specified fines or the hamlet's quota of cloth from market-place shop occupiers.

l: five things, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The five things are policies concerning appointments, market charges, frontier inspections, husbandmen's mutual aid and taxes, and levies on shop occupiers. A ruler who truly practises them will have the support of the people and neighbouring kingdoms.

l: neighbouring kingdoms, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The people in the neighbouring kingdoms will look up to a ruler who truly practises the five things as a parent.

l: enemy, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: A ruler who has no enemy in all the kingdom is described as the minister of Heaven.

l: minister of Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The minister of Heaven is a ruler who has no enemy in the kingdom. Such a ruler will attain the royal dignity.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Heaven is invoked in the title 'minister of Heaven' for a ruler who has no enemy in the kingdom.

l: royal dignity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: A ruler who truly practises the five things and has no enemy in the kingdom will attain the royal dignity.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius explains that all men possess a mind that cannot bear to see others suffer, illustrated by their alarm when a child is about to fall into a well. He says the ancient kings possessed this commiserating mind and practiced commiserating government, making ruling the kingdom easy. He identifies four essential human feelings as principles of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge. He urges men to develop these four principles fully, since their development enables them to love and protect all within the four seas, while their neglect leaves them unable even to serve their parents.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius teaches that all men possess a mind that cannot bear to see the sufferings of others. He explains the four human principles and urges men to develop them fully.

l: men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Humanity possesses four essential principles: commiseration, shame and dislike, modesty and complaisance, and approving and disapproving. These principles can be fully developed to support benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and knowledge.

l: ancient kings, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The ancient kings possessed a commiserating mind and practiced commiserating government.

l: commiserating mind, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The commiserating mind is the inability to bear seeing the sufferings of others. When joined with commiserating government, it makes ruling the kingdom as easy as making anything go round in the palm.

l: commiserating government, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Commiserating government is practiced through a commiserating mind. It makes ruling the kingdom easy.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The kingdom can be ruled as easily as making anything go round in the palm when commiserating government is practiced with a commiserating mind.

l: child, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: A child serves as the example that reveals humanity's natural commiseration when others are in danger.

l: child about to fall into a well, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: When men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they experience alarm and distress without seeking reward, praise, or avoidance of blame.

l: feeling of commiseration, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The feeling of commiseration is essential to man and is the principle of benevolence.

l: feeling of shame and dislike, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The feeling of shame and dislike is essential to man and is the principle of righteousness.

l: feeling of modesty and complaisance, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The feeling of modesty and complaisance is essential to man and is the principle of propriety.

l: feeling of approving and disapproving, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The feeling of approving and disapproving is essential to man and is the principle of knowledge.

l: four principles, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: The four principles are present in all men just as the four limbs are present in them. Men who claim they cannot develop these principles play the thief with themselves, while one who says his prince cannot develop them plays the thief with his prince.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Benevolence is the principle represented by the feeling of commiseration.

l: righteousness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Righteousness is the principle represented by the feeling of shame and dislike.

l: propriety, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Propriety is the principle represented by the feeling of modesty and complaisance.

l: knowledge, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Knowledge is the principle represented by the feeling of approving and disapproving.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius compares the maker of arrows with the maker of armour, noting that each fears the harm associated with his work. He says choosing a profession and a residence requires caution, citing Confucius on the importance of virtuous manners in a neighbourhood. Mencius teaches that benevolence is the honourable dignity conferred by Heaven and the quiet home in which man should dwell. He compares the benevolent person to an archer who seeks the cause of failure in himself rather than blaming others.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Mencius compares the arrow-maker with the maker of armour and says that choosing a profession requires great caution. He teaches that people who fail to practise benevolence should seek the cause of their failure in themselves.

l: Confucius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Confucius says that virtuous manners make a neighbourhood excellent. He teaches that a person who does not choose a residence where such manners prevail is not wise.

l: benevolence, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: Benevolence is described as the most honourable dignity conferred by Heaven and the quiet home in which man should dwell. No one can prevent a person from being benevolent, and lacking benevolence leads to the absence of propriety and righteousness.

l: archer, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 7
s: The archer adjusts himself before shooting. If he misses, he does not blame those who surpass him but turns inward to seek the cause of his failure.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Mencius says that Zi Lu rejoiced when told of his faults, while Yu bowed when he heard good words. Shun delighted in what was good, regarded virtue as common to himself and others, and gave up his own way to follow others. From his early work as a farmer, potter, and fisherman until he became emperor, Shun continually learned from others. Mencius teaches that taking example from others to practise virtue helps them practise it, and that helping men practise virtue is the greatest attribute of the superior man.

l: Zi Lu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Zi Lu rejoiced when anyone told him that he had a fault.

l: Yu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Yu bowed to the speaker when he heard good words.

l: Shun, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Shun had a great delight in what was good and regarded virtue as the common property of himself and others. He gave up his own way to follow that of others and continually learned from others from the time when he ploughed and sowed, exercised the potter's art, and was a fisherman, until he became emperor.

l: others, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Shun gave up his own way to follow the way of others and delighted to learn from others to practise what was good. Taking example from others to practise virtue is said to help them in the same practice.

l: men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Helping men to practise virtue is described as the greatest attribute of the superior man.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: The superior man is characterized above all by helping men to practise virtue.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 8
s: Shun regarded virtue as the common property of himself and others. Practising virtue by taking example from others helps them practise it as well.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius compares Bo Yi and Hui of Liu Xia in their responses to impure princes, bad men, office, poverty, and personal principles. Bo Yi refuses service, association, and gifts connected with people he disapproves of, valuing purity above employment. Hui of Liu Xia serves an impure prince without concealing his virtue, remains steady when neglected or poor, and does not believe proximity to others can defile him. Mencius says Bo Yi was narrow-minded and Hui of Liu Xia lacked self-respect, while the superior man shows neither trait.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius describes Bo Yi's refusal to serve or associate with people he disapproved of and Hui of Liu Xia's willingness to serve an impure prince while maintaining his principles. He says Bo Yi was narrow-minded and Hui of Liu Xia was wanting in self-respect, and that the superior man manifests neither quality.

l: Bo Yi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Bo Yi would not serve a prince he did not approve of or associate with a friend he did not esteem. He refused bad princes, bad men, and gifts from princes when accepting them would conflict with his purity.

l: Hui of Liu Xia, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Hui of Liu Xia was not ashamed to serve an impure prince or to be an inferior officer. He carried out his principles when employed, did not murmur when neglected, did not grieve in poverty, and believed that others could not defile him.

l: princes, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Some princes sent proper messages and offered gifts to Bo Yi, but he would not receive them. Hui of Liu Xia served an impure prince.

l: superior man, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: The superior man will not manifest narrow-mindedness or the want of self-respect.

l: office, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Hui of Liu Xia did not murmur when left without office and would remain in office when pressed to do so. He was willing to serve as an inferior officer.

l: purity, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Bo Yi considered it inconsistent with his purity to go to princes he disapproved of or to accept their gifts. Hui of Liu Xia did not count it required by his purity to leave office when pressed to remain.

l: narrow-mindedness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius says Bo Yi was narrow-minded. The superior man will not manifest narrow-mindedness.

l: self-respect, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 9
s: Mencius says Hui of Liu Xia was wanting in self-respect. The superior man will not manifest the want of self-respect.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Mencius explains that opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven are inferior to advantages of situation afforded by the Earth, which are in turn inferior to the union arising from the accord of Men. He illustrates this with cities that fail to resist attack despite favorable timing or strong defenses. He teaches that a people, State, or kingdom is secured by proper conduct and human support rather than by boundaries, natural defenses, or weapons. He concludes that a true ruler avoids fighting, but must overcome if he fights.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Mencius teaches that opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven, advantages of situation afforded by the Earth, and the union arising from the accord of Men differ in strength, with human accord being greatest. He concludes that the true ruler prefers not to fight but must overcome if he fights.

l: Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Heaven vouchsafes opportunities of time, but those opportunities are not equal to advantages of situation afforded by the Earth.

l: Earth, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: The Earth affords advantages of situation, but those advantages are not equal to the union arising from the accord of Men.

l: men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Men provide the union arising from accord, which is stronger than opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven or advantages of situation afforded by the Earth.

l: opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven can enable an enemy to surround and attack a city, but they do not guarantee that the city will be taken.

l: advantages of situation afforded by the Earth, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: Advantages of situation afforded by the Earth include strong walls, deep moats, effective arms, and abundant stores. They can still fail to preserve a city when the union arising from the accord of Men is lacking.

l: union arising from the accord of Men, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: The union arising from the accord of Men is presented as stronger than opportunities of time vouchsafed by Heaven and advantages of situation afforded by the Earth. It enables a ruler to receive broad assistance and obedience.

l: people below, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: A people is bounded in not by the limits of dykes and borders but by principles concerning proper rule and support.

l: State, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: A State is secured not by the strengths of mountains and rivers but by principles concerning proper rule and support.

l: kingdom, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: A kingdom is overawed not by the sharpness and strength of arms. When many assist the ruler, the whole kingdom becomes obedient to the prince.

l: proper course, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: He who finds the proper course has many to assist him, while he who loses it has few to assist him. When support is reduced to its extreme, his own relations revolt from the prince.

l: prince, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 1
s: The prince receives obedience from the whole kingdom when many assist him. When few assist him, his own relations revolt from him; if he attacks those whose relations revolt, he must overcome.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius declines the king of Qi’s request to attend court, saying he is unwell, but visits a condolence gathering the next day. When questioned by Gong Sun Chou and Jing Chou, Mencius defends his conduct and says that presenting benevolence and righteousness to the king is the greatest respect he can show him. He argues that virtue, age, and nobility are the three universally acknowledged honors, and that rulers who seek great achievements should learn from virtuous ministers rather than command them. Tang’s treatment of Yi Yin and the duke Huan’s treatment of Guan Zhong are given as examples of rulers who first learned from those ministers and then employed them.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Mencius declines to attend the king’s court because he says he is unwell, though he visits a member of the Dong Guo family the next day. He later explains to Jing Chou that speaking to the king about the ways of Yao and Shun is the greatest respect he can show him, and that a prince seeking great deeds should go to virtuous ministers rather than summon them.

l: king (king of Qi), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The king sends word that he wishes to see Mencius but has a cold and plans to hold court the next morning. He sends a messenger and a physician to inquire about Mencius’s illness and asks that Mencius come to court before returning home.

l: Gong Sun Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Gong Sun Chou questions Mencius about declining to attend court because of illness while visiting someone in condolence the next day.

l: Jing Chou, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Jing Chou tells Mencius that respect governs the relationship between prince and minister and says he has seen the king respect Mencius but not how Mencius respects the king. He challenges Mencius’s failure to carry out his intended court visit after hearing the king’s order.

l: the philosopher Zeng, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The philosopher Zeng says that the wealth and nobility of Jin and Chu cannot equal his own benevolence and righteousness. Mencius cites these sentiments as expressing a real principle.

l: Tang, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Tang first learned from Yi Yin and then employed him as his minister, thereby becoming sovereign without difficulty.

l: Yi Yin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Yi Yin is presented as a virtuous teacher whom Tang first learned from and then employed as his minister.

l: the duke Huan, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The duke Huan first learned from Guan Zhong and then employed him as his minister, thereby becoming chief of all the princes without difficulty.

l: Guan Zhong, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Guan Zhong is presented as a minister from whom the duke Huan first learned. Mencius says that if Guan Zhong could not be summoned by his prince, still less could someone who would not play Guan Zhong’s part be summoned.

l: benevolence and righteousness, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The people of Qi do not speak to the king about benevolence and righteousness because they believe he is not fit to be spoken with about them. Mencius says he presents the ways of Yao and Shun to the king and regards benevolence and righteousness as possessions equal to wealth and nobility.

l: respect, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Respect governs the relationship between prince and minister. Mencius says that speaking to the king about benevolence and righteousness demonstrates greater respect than remaining silent because the king is thought unfit to hear about them.

l: virtue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: Virtue is one of the three universally acknowledged honors, along with nobility and age. In helping one’s generation and presiding over the people, virtue is greater than the other two.

l: the court visit, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 2
s: The planned court visit is declined by Mencius when he says he is unwell. Although he later goes out to pay a visit of condolence, he is pressed to go to Jing Chou’s and spend the night there rather than immediately return home.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Chen Zhen questions Mencius about accepting or refusing presents sent to him in Qi, Song, and Xue. Mencius says he did right in all three cases because the presents served different purposes. In Song, the present was for travelling expenses, and in Xue, it was to help procure arms for protection. In Qi, he had no need for money, so accepting the present would have been accepting a bribe.

l: Chen Zhen, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Chen Zhen asks Mencius to explain why he refused a present in Qi but accepted presents in Song and Xue.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius says he acted rightly in all three cases. He accepted money in Song for travelling expenses and in Xue to help procure arms, but refused it in Qi because he had no need for money.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: In Qi, Mencius had no occasion for money and refused the present sent to him.

l: Song, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: In Song, Mencius was about to take a long journey and accepted a present intended for travelling expenses.

l: Xue, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: In Xue, Mencius was apprehensive for his safety and accepted a present intended to help him procure arms.

l: present (present sent to Mencius), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Presents were sent to Mencius in Qi, Song, and Xue. Their stated purposes were travelling expenses in Song and procuring arms in Xue.

l: money, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Money was accepted by Mencius when it was needed for travelling expenses or protection, but he refused it in Qi because he had no occasion for it.

l: bribe, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 3
s: Mencius says that sending a man a gift when he has no occasion for it is to bribe him. He says a superior man should not be taken with a bribe.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius confronts the governor of Ping Lu, Kong Ju Xin, about repeatedly failing to protect the people under his charge. He compares the governor’s duty to that of a herder responsible for finding pasture for cattle and sheep. Kong Ju Xin admits his guilt, and Mencius later tells the king that Kong Ju Xin is the only governor who knows his faults. The king accepts responsibility and says that he is guilty in this matter.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Mencius addresses Kong Ju Xin in Ping Lu about the deaths and displacement of the people during bad calamitous years and years of famine. He later tells the king that Kong Ju Xin is the only governor among five who knows his faults.

l: Ping Lu, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Ping Lu is the place where Mencius addresses its governor about failures in caring for its people.

l: Kong Ju Xin, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: Kong Ju Xin is the governor addressed by Mencius. He says that the situation is not his responsibility, but after Mencius compares his duty to caring for cattle and sheep, he admits that he is guilty.

l: king, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: The king hears Mencius repeat his conversation with Kong Ju Xin and says that he is guilty in this matter.

l: people (Ping Lu's people), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: During bad calamitous years and years of famine, the old and feeble among Ping Lu's people are found lying in ditches and water-channels, while the able-bodied are scattered to the four quarters, numbering several thousand.

l: bad calamitous years, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: During bad calamitous years, the old and feeble of Ping Lu's people are found lying in ditches and water-channels, and the able-bodied are scattered to the four quarters.

l: years of famine, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 4
s: During years of famine, the old and feeble of Ping Lu's people are found lying in ditches and water-channels, and the able-bodied are scattered to the four quarters.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius questions Qi Wa about declining the governorship of Ling Qiu and becoming chief criminal judge so he could speak his views. After several months, Qi Wa remonstrates with the king, resigns when his counsel is ignored, and leaves. The people of Qi approve Mencius’s guidance to Qi Wa but question Qi Wa’s own conduct. Mencius explains that he is free to advance or retire because he holds no office and bears no duty to give his opinion.

l: Mencius, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Mencius questions Qi Wa about whether he has found anything to speak about after becoming chief criminal judge. He later explains that people responsible for an office or for giving opinions should leave when their duties cannot be fulfilled or their words are ignored, but that he may act freely because he holds no office and has no such duty.

l: Qi Wa, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: Qi Wa declines the governorship of Ling Qiu and requests appointment as chief criminal judge so he can speak his views. He remonstrates with the king, resigns when his counsel is not accepted, and leaves.

l: Qi, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The people of Qi say that Mencius did well in the course he marked out for Qi Wa, but they do not know whether Qi Wa follows the same course for himself.

l: course of action, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: The course marked out for Qi Wa is viewed by the people of Qi as good, while Qi Wa’s own course is questioned.

l: giving one's opinion, Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 5
s: A person responsible for giving an opinion should leave when their words are not attended to. Mencius says that no duty of giving his opinion devolves on him because he holds no office.

l: Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Mencius, Book II (Gong Sun Chou), Chapter 6
s: Mencius, a high dignitary in Qi, went to Teng on a mission of condolence. The king sent Wang Huan, the governor of Gai, as assistant-commissioner. Wang Huan attended Mencius morning and evening, but Mencius did not discuss the mission's business with him during the journey there and back. Mencius explained that proper officers handled those matters.
